answer_text:
Let  
\[
f(z)=\frac{z^2}{(z^2+4)(z^4-1)}.
\]

There is an important subtlety: \(f\) has simple poles at \(x=\pm1\) on the real axis, so the integral is **not convergent as an ordinary improper integral**. The residue theorem with an indented contour evaluates its **Cauchy principal value**.

Poles:
\[
z=\pm1,\quad z=\pm i,\quad z=\pm 2i.
\]
In the upper half-plane we have \(z=i\) and \(z=2i\), while the real poles \(z=\pm1\) are indented.

Residues:
\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,1)=\frac{1}{20},\qquad
\operatorname{Res}(f,-1)=-\frac{1}{20},
\]
so their sum is \(0\).

For the upper-half-plane poles:
\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,i)
=\frac{i^2}{(i^2+4)(4i^3)}
=\frac{-1}{3(-4i)}
=-\frac{i}{12},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)
=\frac{(2i)^2}{(2(2i))((2i)^4-1)}
=\frac{-4}{4i\cdot 15}
=\frac{i}{15}.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,i)+\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)
=-\frac{i}{12}+\frac{i}{15}
=-\frac{i}{60}.
\]

Using an upper half-plane contour with small upper indentations around the real poles, the large arc contributes \(0\) because \(f(z)=O(z^{-4})\). The indentation contributions vanish since
\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,1)+\operatorname{Res}(f,-1)=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx
=2\pi i\left(-\frac{i}{60}\right)
=\frac{\pi}{30}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{(x^2+4)(x^4-1)}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{30}}
\]

Without the principal-value interpretation, the integral diverges because of the poles at \(x=\pm1\).
